This page contains a list of tools and commands I find particularly useful.

## Reading and writing

### Document writing

I never got into the Microsoft Office suite of tools that includes Word. I've previously had to use Word for work and I struggle to find much good to say about it.

I do the majority of my writing (including this website and blog) in [Markdown](https://daringfireball.net/projects/Markdown/), or [Quarto](https://quarto.org), which is basically also Markdown! Some of the benefits of writing in Markdown are that it's intuitive, readable, flexible, future proof, interoperable with many other programmes, and it allows you to focus on content. Plus it's the *lingua franca* of AI, and it's now even [supported by Google Docs](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/10/preview-edit-and-collaborate-on-Markdown-files-natively-across-Drive-and-Docs.html) for collaborative editing! If I *really* need to get a Word document out of the end, I use either [Pandoc](http://pandoc.org/) or [Quarto](https://quarto.org). See [useful commands](#useful-terminal-commands) below for how to use this.

### Note taking

I store most of my notes in the truly excellent [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/). Obsidian is a clean text Markdown-based note-taking system that separates the data (Markdown files) from the viewer/editor in a way that means you always stay in control of your own data. I've found Microsoft [OneNote](https://www.onenote.com/) to be good too, but it's a bit less configurable, even if the app support across surfaces is excellent.

### Text/code editor

I use Microsoft's [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) (with the Markdown all in one and Markdown preview enhanced extensions) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/).

### Writing papers

For papers, I've switched to using Markdown/[Quarto](https://quarto.org). You can find a [cookie-cutter research template with paper and slides here](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookiecutter-research-project). You can insert figures, tables, *and* numbers into text, including in-line, so that the paper and slides can be completely updated if the results change. That makes it perfect for reproducible analytical pipelines. You can also export to LaTeX. I still use LaTeX from time to time. Although Visual Studio Code has a LaTeX editor that's very good, I use [TeXshop](https://pages.uoregon.edu/koch/texshop/) for LaTeX editing.

### Reading papers

I store papers in [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/), which is an open source endeavour. You can support them by paying for their storage. They have an excellent iPad app too. Even better, [you can sync your papers and notes with Obsidian](../blog/posts/til-zotero-and-obsidian/index.md).

## Coding and development

- *Version control*. I use [git](https://git-scm.com/) and [GitHub](https://github.com/).
- *Development environment*. I use [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) for almost all code, including Python and R. (I wrote a post about how to set it up for R [here](../blog/posts/setting-up-r-in-vscode/index.md).) I also use Docker for development, including the excellent Visual Studio Code docker extensions.
- *Cloud compute*. When I need cloud capabilities, I mostly go for [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/), connecting via Visual Studio Code remote (instructions in [this post](../blog/posts/visual-studio-code-in-the-cloud/index.md).)
- *Package manager*. To install things sensibly on a Mac, I use [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/).
- *Terminal*:
    - [ghostty](https://ghostty.org/) for my terminal
    - [ohmyzsh](https://ohmyz.sh/) for zsh configuration
    - [ohmyposh](https://ohmyposh.dev/) as a prompt engine
    - [lsd](https://github.com/lsd-rs/lsd) as a replacement for `ls`
    - [wget](https://www.gnu.org/software/wget/) for downloads
    - [ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep) for text-in-file search
    - [llm](https://github.com/simonw/llm) to run local and remote large language models
    - [duckdb -ui](https://duckdb.org/2025/03/12/duckdb-ui) for exploring SQL databases
    - [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/) for converting audio and video
    - [imagemagick](https://imagemagick.org/) for working with image files
    - [f2](https://github.com/ayoisaiah/f2) for bulk renaming files
    - [Inkscape](https://inkscape.org/) on the command line, mainly for converting things to svg 
- *Programming language*. My default is Python, for a whole host of reasons, with, of course, some SQL. I am a huge convert to [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and now use it to install Python, build packages, and manage repo packages.
- *Building Python packages*. There's [a template for that](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookiecutter-python-package)!
- *Hardware*. I use a MacBook Pro with an M5 Max chip, an amazing laptop.

## Communication

- *Slide shows*. My preference is to use written notes over slide decks whenever possible (you can read a bit more about why [here](../blog/posts/managing-public-sector-knowledge/managing-public-sector-knowledge.qmd#notes-should-be-the-default-with-microsoft-powerpoint-presentations-only-by-exception)), following the [Amazon model](https://www.managementtoday.co.uk/why-amazon-banned-powerpoint/leadership-lessons/article/1689543). But you need a slide show now and again! If it's leaning toward a general audience and it covers a wide range of topics, I'll typically use [Keynote](https://www.apple.com/uk/keynote/). I know it isn't cross-platform, but you can create something that looks good in it quickly and easily—and you can export every stage of builds to PDF too. For giving talks on research papers, I used to reach for [beamer](https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer) and LaTeX but I now use [Quarto for slides](https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/) because everything can be programmatically re-generated if results change, it plays nicely with code chunks and code execution, and the HTML slides you can create are pretty nice. Again, check out the research project template [here](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookiecutter-research-project)
- *Website*. I use [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) and [Github pages](https://pages.github.com/), a powerful combination. For the website code, I'm indebted to [Andrew Heiss](https://www.andrewheiss.com/) for making the code for his website available.

## Misc

- For graphics, I normally go for [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/), which is so much more powerful than most people realise. All of the graphics in my book [The Star Builders](../thestarbuilders/thestarbuilders.qmd) were created using matplotlib. If I need a manual programme for graphics, I normally use [Inkscape](https://inkscape.org/), which is much better on Mac than it once was.
- I keep track of tasks with the excellent [Things](https://culturedcode.com/things/) (Mac).
- For fonts, [Nerd Fonts](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) is good, as are the [GitHub ones](https://github.com/githubnext/monaspace). For a much wider selection, there's always [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/).

## Useful terminal commands

For most of these, you'll need to download the tools first.

### Pandoc

With Pandoc, a line

```bash
pandoc briefing.md -V geometry:margin=0.2in --standalone \
--bibliography references.bib --citeproc --csl=harvard.csl -o briefing.docx
```

applied to a file called "briefing.md", a bibtex file of references ("references.bib"), and a citation style (here "harvard.csl") will produce a Word document called "briefing.docx". It's fairly similar to using [Quarto to generate a Word document](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/ms-word.html). For more elaborate documents, like a book manuscript, I've created a couple of helper tools like [this quarto template](https://github.com/aeturrell/cookie-cutter-quarto-book-manuscript).

### Magic(k) to create webp files from PDFs

```bash
magick -density 300 your_pdf.pdf \
  -background white -alpha remove -alpha off \
  -define webp:lossless=true \
  output_image.webp
```

### Magic(k)ing .HEIC files to jpgs

```bash
magick mogrify -format jpg *.HEIC
```

### ffmpeg mov to mp4

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.mov output.mp4
```

### One-line PDF to text

```bash
uvx docling path-to-your-pdf
```

### One-line parquet file data summary

```bash
uvx skimpy some_data.parquet
```

### Find string in text files

eg for .qmd files only

```bash
rg "<phrase>" -g "*.qmd"
```

### Interactive search results found in text files

```bash
rg "import pandas" --type py | fzf
```

I usually have an alias for this, `rgf`. To set this up on Mac, you'll need to `brew install` [**rg**](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep), [**bat**](https://github.com/sharkdp/bat), and [**fzf**](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf). Then add the following to your `.zshrc` file, if you're using ZSH (amend according to your setup.) You can open the file in an editor with `code ~/.zshrc`. Then add this to the end of the file:

```bash
# ripgrep + fzf interactive search → VS Code
rgf() {
  local result
  result=$(
    rg --color=always --line-number --no-heading --smart-case "$@" |
      fzf --ansi \
          --delimiter : \
          --preview 'bat --color=always --highlight-line {2} --map-syntax "*.qmd:Markdown" {1}' \
          --preview-window 'up,60%,border-bottom,+{2}+3/3,~3'
  )
  if [[ -n "$result" ]]; then
    local file line
    file=$(echo "$result" | cut -d: -f1)
    line=$(echo "$result" | cut -d: -f2)
    code --goto "${file}:${line}"
  fi
}
```

Now you can use commands like

```bash
rgf "import pandas" -g "*.qmd"
```

to interactively, fuzzily, and quickly search your files.

### Bulk renaming

```bash
f2 -f '\(2021\)' -r '[2022]'
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
| ORIGINAL                             | RENAMED                              | STATUS |
| ************************************************************************************ |
| No Pressure (2021) S01.E01.2160p.mp4 | No Pressure [2022] S01.E01.2160p.mp4 | ok     |
| No Pressure (2021) S01.E02.2160p.mp4 | No Pressure [2022] S01.E02.2160p.mp4 | ok     |
| No Pressure (2021) S01.E03.2160p.mp4 | No Pressure [2022] S01.E03.2160p.mp4 | ok     |
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### System monitoring

Basic (built in):

```bash
top
```

Much more detail and easier to read (but requires install):

```bash
bpytop
```

### Merging PDFs

See [this blog post.](../blog/posts/til-merging-pdfs/index.qmd)

### Unwrapping markdown

Editing wrapped markdown is a bit of a pain, so I tend to use completely unwrapped markdown and have the IDE / user interface provide visual wrapping that doesn't change the underlying file. Sometimes, though, you come across an annoyingly wrapped markdown file. In which case...

```bash
uvx panache format -o wrap=reflow -o line-width=100000 path/to/file.qmd
```

## Pre-commit heroes

Some tools I've found useful as part of a [pre-commit configuration](https://pre-commit.com).

### Panache

"[Panache](https://panache.bz) is a language server, formatter, and linter for Quarto and other Markdown flavors, including Pandoc, R Markdown, and MyST. It is written in Rust and understands syntax that generic Markdown tools often miss, including fenced divs, tables, and math."

Panache does markdown + code block syntax formatting, which is why I like it. Unfortunately it doesn't currently support Jupyter notebooks.

### Ruff for Python formatting, linting, and sorting

Formatting:

```bash
ruff format path/to/code/
```

Linting

```bash
ruff check path/to/code/
```

Sorting imports

```bash
ruff check --select I --fix .
```

### Stripping output content from Jupyter notebooks

[NBStripout](https://github.com/kynan/nbstripout) is the tool for this!

### An example pre-commit config

To use this, you'll need to run

```bash
uv add --group dev ruff pydoclint panache-cli nbstripout pre-commit-hooks
```

to install the dependencies first.

`.pre-commit-config.yaml`:

```text
# Every hook runs from the project's own environment via `uv run`, so tool
# versions come from pyproject.toml (constraints) and uv.lock (exact pins).
#
# `--frozen` runs against uv.lock as-is (no re-resolve on every commit);
# the `uv-lock` hook below is what catches a stale lockfile.
#
# Requires uv on PATH. Install with: uv run pre-commit install
minimum_pre_commit_version: "4.4.0" # for `language: unsupported`
default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit]
default_stages: [pre-commit, manual]

repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      # --- Lockfile ------------------------------------------------------
      - id: uv-lock
        name: Check uv.lock is up to date
        entry: uv lock --check
        language: unsupported
        files: ^(pyproject\.toml|uv\.lock)$
        pass_filenames: false

      # --- Python: lint, then format (order matters) ----------------------
      # Import sorting is ruff's "I" rules, enabled in pyproject.toml.
      # --force-exclude makes ruff honour its own excludes for passed files.
      - id: ruff-check
        name: ruff check
        entry: uv run --frozen ruff check --fix --force-exclude
        language: unsupported
        types_or: [python, pyi, jupyter]
        require_serial: true

      - id: ruff-format
        name: ruff format
        entry: uv run --frozen ruff format --force-exclude
        language: unsupported
        types_or: [python, pyi, jupyter]
        require_serial: true

      # Style and excludes come from [tool.pydoclint] in pyproject.toml.
      - id: pydoclint
        name: pydoclint
        entry: uv run --frozen pydoclint
        language: unsupported
        types: [python]
        files: ^src/

      # --- Quarto ---------------------------------------------------------
      # Formats Python cells in .qmd files with Ruff; prose is not reflowed.
      # Settings live in panache.toml. Runs under `uv run`, so the `ruff` it
      # calls is the locked one from the project environment.
      - id: panache-format
        name: panache format (Quarto)
        entry: uv run --frozen panache format
        language: unsupported
        files: \.qmd$

      # --- Notebooks -----------------------------------------------------
      - id: nbstripout
        name: Strip notebook outputs
        entry: uv run --frozen nbstripout
        language: unsupported
        types: [jupyter]

      # --- Project-specific ----------------------------------------------
      - id: check-python-versions
        name: Check supported Python versions agree
        entry: uv run --frozen python scripts/check_python_versions.py
        language: unsupported
        files: ^(pyproject\.toml|noxfile\.py|\.python-version)$
        pass_filenames: false

      # --- General file hygiene (from the pre-commit-hooks package) ------
      - id: check-added-large-files
        name: Check for added large files
        entry: uv run --frozen check-added-large-files
        language: unsupported

      - id: check-merge-conflict
        name: Check for merge conflict markers
        entry: uv run --frozen check-merge-conflict
        language: unsupported
        types: [text]

      - id: check-case-conflict
        name: Check for case-insensitive filename conflicts
        entry: uv run --frozen check-case-conflict
        language: unsupported

      - id: debug-statements
        name: Check for debugger imports and breakpoints
        entry: uv run --frozen debug-statement-hook
        language: unsupported
        types: [python]

      - id: check-toml
        name: Check TOML
        entry: uv run --frozen check-toml
        language: unsupported
        types: [toml]

      - id: check-yaml
        name: Check YAML
        entry: uv run --frozen check-yaml
        language: unsupported
        types: [yaml]
        exclude: ^docs/

      - id: end-of-file-fixer
        name: Fix end of files
        entry: uv run --frozen end-of-file-fixer
        language: unsupported
        types: [text]
        exclude: ^docs/

      - id: trailing-whitespace
        name: Trim trailing whitespace
        entry: uv run --frozen trailing-whitespace-fixer
        language: unsupported
        types: [text]
        exclude: ^docs/

      - id: mixed-line-ending
        name: Normalise line endings to LF
        entry: uv run --frozen mixed-line-ending --fix=lf
        language: unsupported
        types: [text]
        exclude: ^docs/

```

Inside `pyproject.toml`:

```text
...

[tool.pydoclint]
style = 'google'
exclude = ["noxfile.py", "tests/", "docs/"]

[tool.ruff.lint]
# Ruff defaults (E4, E7, E9, F) plus import sorting.
extend-select = ["I"]

...
```

And `panache.toml` (panache needs its own config file because it doesn't support `pyproject.toml` configurations):

```text
#:schema https://panache.bz/panache.schema.json
# Panache formats Quarto (.qmd) files. Prose is left as written: the only
# substantive change is running Ruff over Python code cells. Ruff's own
# settings come from [tool.ruff] in pyproject.toml.
flavor = "quarto"

[format]
wrap = "preserve"               # keep authored line breaks; never reflow prose
math = "verbatim"               # don't restructure LaTeX inside $...$ / $$...$$
math-delimiter-style = "preserve"

[formatters]
python = "ruff"                 # runs `ruff format -` on {python} / python blocks
```
